findings.where: Article specimen, 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law': the body paragraphs, the subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?', the numbered list and the closing paragraph, at both widths
findings.fault: The whole article is centred. Every paragraph has a ragged left edge, so the eye has to find where each line starts. In the numbered list the wrapped lines centre under their item, which pulls the text away from its number by a different amount on each line (items 2 and 3 start far to the right of their numbers). The list looks broken, not set. This is the one place the brief asks the look to prove it survives Angélique's content (an image, a caption, a list, a subhead), and the list is where it visibly fails.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked that the article specimen show the rhythm holding with a list and a subhead, and who treats the article and the PDF list as the product. Development-bank readers who come to read Mark's argument would also object: centred long-form text and a misaligned list read as an amateur blog, not a legal journal.

findings.where: First screen, Mark's photograph on the right half (desktop), and the same photograph above the line (phone)
findings.fault: The v7 direction is 'Mark at work', a full-bleed photograph of him speaking at an event. Here the photograph's backdrop is keyed out, and the lectern and event are lost apart from the tip of a microphone. What remains is a very large cut-out head floating on flat slate. At this scale the face outweighs his line when you squint, and the hero reads as a candidate's campaign poster, not an advisor caught at work. The direction's lever, real setting and real light, is gone, so the tile is hard to tell apart from v6's portrait or v4's dark ground.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging this tile as the 'Mark at work' direction against the six others: its distinguishing idea doesn't show. Mark would object too, given his wish for a refined look that is not salesy or slick, because a giant floating head pushes the page towards a promotional poster.

findings.where: First screen, around the 'Write to me directly' action
findings.fault: Nothing on the first screen is checkable. There is no place, year, named event or body next to the action, and the one piece of evidence the photograph carried (that he was speaking at a real event) has been keyed away. A visitor is asked to write before seeing any sign that Mark has done this kind of work for organisations like theirs, in their region.
findings.who_objects: Staff at a development bank arriving from LinkedIn, who select individuals against terms of reference and need one concrete sign of relevant work before writing. First-visit trust says this proof sits next to the main action, and Feel the CV asks for a photo at a named event.

findings.fault: Each specimen section opens with a different kind of heading: tracked capitals for Palette, a small bold sans for Type pair and Motion sketch, and a large italic serif for Texture. Sections that are parallel don't look parallel, so the specimen reads as pieces assembled separately, not one system. The tracked capitals on 'PALETTE' also contradict the page's own type note ('Sentence case, never tracked capitals').
findings.who_objects: The founder, reading the style tile to judge whether this direction holds together as one identity. A tile whose own labels break its stated rules weakens the case it makes.

findings.where: First screen, top-left lockup 'Mark M. Moseley | MMM INFRA' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The white aqueduct mark is far larger and heavier than Mark's name beside it, so when you squint the firm's logo leads and his name reads as its caption. The brief's personal-advisor test says his name leads, with the logo beside it.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Mark, for whom 'the individual is the brand' and 'the firm is the brand' fails. The lockup's weight says the opposite of the order the brief asks for.
